newsitem.title: FRANCE: France mulls checks on media cover of legal probes.
newsitem.headline: France mulls checks on media cover of legal probes.

text.p: A report for France's justice minister recommended on Tuesday a tightening of sub-judice laws that would require media reports of investigations to mention that they were based on the author's "personal opinion".

Sub-judice laws have been widely flouted by the French media, often with the complicity of investigating magistrates who use publicity to ensure their probes into political corruption, among other sensitive offences, are not buried.
Justice Minister Jacques Toubon told a news conference that the report, sought by the government last year, was aimed at fuelling a reform of legal procedures but "does not commit the government".
Toubon, who put foward the report which seeks to boost the presumption of innocence, said the ruling centre-right coalition would take decisions on the reform in coming months.

The report recommends that anyone referring to a penal investigation must include a mention in his or her report "to draw people's attention to the fact that the information in question expresses only the author's personal opinion".

The report by law professor Michele-Laure Rassat also suggests creating two new offences of "communication" and "publication" on procedural acts and carrying a two-year professional suspension and a 300,000 franc ($60,000) fine respectively.
"I'm an ultra-liberal as far as procedure goes...But freedom goes with responsibility," she said.

Judge Renaud van Ruymbeke, who has pioneered probes into political corruption, advocated a wide-ranging reform of the judicial system to strip the government of its control over public prosecutors and investigating magistrates.

"Everyone muast have the right to a public trial within a reasonable delay," he told France-2 television. "The problem in France is that political authorities (through the justice ministry) have power over public prosecutors.

"That means that investigating magistrates act differently from the public prosecutors," he said in a veiled reference to political attempts to block sensitive inquiries and to the appointment of political cronies as prosecutors. "Today's system is totally hypocritical," he added.
Rassat also suggested limiting detention for those awaiting a trial to six months at the most, and giving someone other than a judge power to detain suspects threatening public order.
Critics have accused some magistrates leading probes into alleged fraud by business and political establishment figures of using preventive detention to try and make suspects confess.
